blogs.title: The Staleness Trap: How *Farahi* Resolves the Tension Between FOIA Delays and Ongoing Investigations
blogs.description: This post analyzes the D.C. Circuit's handling of the temporal gap between the FBI's initial 2019 summary judgment motion and the 2023 appellate review. It examines how the court navigated the precedent set in *CREW v. DOJ* regarding 'stale' declarations, ultimately ruling that a terse update declaration can suffice when viewed as a supplement to a detailed, earlier ex parte submission rather than a standalone proof. The analysis will explore the practical implications for litigants facing multi-year FOIA delays in national security contexts, suggesting that courts may increasingly rely on the 'totality of the record' to validate ongoing investigations even when recent public affidavits lack specificity.

blogs.title: Beyond Word Counts: The Expanding Scope of 'Reasonable Segregability' in Counterterrorism Files
blogs.description: Focusing on Part V of the opinion, this article dissects the court's rejection of Farahi's argument that the sheer volume of withheld records (over 10,000 pages) necessitates some releasable content. The post will critique the application of the 'inextricably intertwined' doctrine, where the court affirmed that non-exempt words scattered line-by-line do not constitute 'meaningful information' worthy of segregation. This ruling reinforces a high bar for plaintiffs challenging wholesale withholdings in complex intelligence files, effectively allowing agencies to argue that context is so pervasive that redacting specific data points would reveal nothing of substantive value while still compromising investigative methods.

blogs.title: The Invisible Adversary: Procedural Fairness and the Normalization of Ex Parte Evidence in FOIA Litigation
blogs.description: This piece explores the procedural dimensions of *Farahi*, specifically the heavy reliance on ex parte, under-seal declarations to resolve both the exemption applicability and segregability issues. By noting Farahi's failure to object to the procedure below and citing *Perioperative Services*, the D.C. Circuit signals a continued deference to executive branch secrecy mechanisms when national security is invoked. The post will discuss the growing asymmetry in FOIA litigation, where plaintiffs are increasingly forced to challenge government assertions without seeing the underlying evidence, raising critical questions about adversarial testing and due process in the nation's capital circuit.
